doc.title: Gerald Wiggins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 2, 1995

title: State of jazz, early bop, Monroe's Uptown House and Benny Carter
summary: He compares today's youngsters to the bop generation, recalls Dizzy's early bop around Monroe's versus Minton's, and joining Benny Carter.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: What do you think of the state of jazz today?

It’s the same as it’s always been with youngsters coming up with new ideas. I know when — I’m from more or less the bop era, and the older guys didn’t understand what we were doing and we didn’t know what we were doing either, but we were doing something you know? It evolved into bop. Well the kids are doing the same thing now. They want their own voice and their own sound and that’s what they’re doing. Now you can either like it or not like it, but it’s here, and it’s not going away.
Yeah. And if you don’t like it you don’t have to listen to it.

So well yeah, but I found out you have to listen to find out what they’re doing. And it’s new so it’s strange, so you have to get used to — give it a good listen and find out what they’re doing. I know the first time I heard bop well I’d been around Dizzy quite a bit, so he was just getting it together, you know with the flat fives and raised ninths. And nobody knew what he was doing. He used to drive little trumpet players crazy. I was working in a place called Monroe’s Uptown House and we had two trumpet players: Vic Coulson and Joe Treadwell who later married Sarah Vaughan. They bought themselves a couple of cornets and it was terrible to hear them try to play like Diz, I mean they were in bad shape. But they tried.
Wasn’t that the place where Thelonious Monk was doing some of that early —
No that was downtown. That was, oh what was the name of that joint? But Monroe’s Uptown House was in Harlem, about 134th or 135th Street. But the place you’re talking about, how can I forget it?
Minton’s. Minton’s Playhouse, yeah. That’s where Monk was.

Did you notice when jazz moved from the Swing Era I guess into the bop, when bop became real popular, was there a loss of audience? Or did that affect your career at all? I mean the music changed drastically after World War II.

Well I joined Benny Carter about that time. And I was kidding him I says, “Are we going to start playing bop?” And he says, “Well you’re playing it already.” I said, “Oh, good.” Benny Carter had a big influence on my career because he’s a superhuman guy. That guy is unbelievable. He can write, he can play, and he’s a nice man which helps a lot you know.
